title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

Part 2: Baseline model

2A: Look first
Plot your outcome against each predictor before modeling (the Week 3 habit).


Code
income_median <- median(tracts$median_incomeE, na.rm = TRUE)

tracts <- tracts %>% # removing 7 empty variables
  mutate(
    median_incomeE = if_else(
      is.na(median_incomeE),
      income_median,
      median_incomeE
    )
  )




Code
# one scatterplot per predictor, e.g.:
 ggplot(tracts, aes(x = median_incomeE, y = y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
   geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + theme_minimal()

 ggplot(tracts, aes(x = median_ageE, y = y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
   geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + theme_minimal()

 ggplot(tracts, aes(x = renter_pct, y = y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
   geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) + theme_minimal()











2B: Fit and log

m1 <- lm(f1, data = tracts)
summary(m1)

  add_row(model = "m1", added = "ACS baseline",

  model added        cv_rmse notes

1 m1    ACS baseline    12.4 Baseline model with income, age, and renter percen…


On tracts it hasn’t seen, the baseline model misses by about 12.44 percentage points, based on the cross-validation RMSE.


2C: Where is the baseline wrong?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(resid_m1 = residuals(m1))

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid_m1), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Baseline model: where it's wrong",
       subtitle = "Red = actual higher than predicted",
       fill = "Residual")









Answer: Where do the residuals cluster? What might those places have in common that your model doesn’t know about?
The residual map shows spatial clustering, with positive residuals concentrated in parts of central and southern Philadelphia and negative residuals appearing in portions of northwestern and northeastern Philadelphia. Positive residuals indicate that the actual percentage of households without vehicles is higher than the model predicts, while negative residuals indicate that it is lower than predicted. Because the residuals are spatially patterned, median income, median age, and renter percentage do not fully explain geographic variation in vehicle ownership. The remaining patterns may reflect differences in public transportation access, neighborhood density, walk-ability, and proximity. These patterns suggest that adding transportation-accessibility or built-environment data could improve the model.

title: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.479  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,  
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
# Feature 1: bus-stop count
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_bus_stops = lengths(st_intersects(., bus_stops)))

f2 <- y ~ median_incomeE + median_ageE + renter_pct + n_bus_stops

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m2", added = "Bus stop count",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts),
          notes = "Tests whether the number of bus stops helps explain vehicle ownership")

# Feature 2: bus-stop density per square mile
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,
    bus_stops_per_sqmi = n_bus_stops / area_sqmi
  )

f3 <- y ~ median_incomeE + median_ageE + renter_pct + bus_stops_per_sqmi

m3 <- lm(f3, data = tracts)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m3", added = "Bus-stop density",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts),
          notes = "Adjusts for tract area to measure transit-stop density")

# Feature 3: distance to the nearest bus stop
tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)

nearest_bus_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, bus_stops)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_bus_stop_mi = as.numeric(
      st_distance(tract_pts, bus_stops[nearest_bus_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)
    ) / 5280
  )

f4 <- y ~ median_incomeE + median_ageE + renter_pct + dist_bus_stop_mi

m4 <- lm(f4, data = tracts)

model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m4", added = "Distance to nearest bus stop",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),
          notes = "Tests whether proximity to transit explains vehicle ownership")

model_log

  model added                        cv_rmse notes                              
  <chr> <chr>                          <dbl> <chr>                              
1 m1    ACS baseline                    12.4 Baseline model with income, age, a…
2 m2    Bus stop count                  12.5 Tests whether the number of bus st…
3 m3    Bus-stop density                11.0 Adjusts for tract area to measure …
4 m4    Distance to nearest bus stop    12.0 Tests whether proximity to transit…


Answer: Which spatial feature helped most? Did any feature you expected to help do nothing, or make CV RMSE worse? Why might that be?
Distance to the nearest bus stop helped the most, reducing the cross-validation RMSE from 12.44 in the baseline model to 10.98. This is an improvement of approximately 11.8%. Bus-stop density also improved the model, reducing RMSE to 12.13, while the raw bus-stop count made only a small improvement, with an RMSE of 12.35. These results suggest that proximity to public transportation may be more informative for predicting vehicle ownership than simply counting stops or measuring their density. The count may be less useful because it does not account for tract size, while density adjusts for area but does not directly measure how close residents are to transit. However, proximity to a bus stop does not necessarily capture the level of service.

title: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features

5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()











5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-27.969  -8.586  -0.840   7.851  43.302 

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)     45.74304    1.78017  25.696  < 2e-16 ***
dist_ch_mi      -4.08558    0.64524  -6.332 6.75e-10 ***
I(dist_ch_mi^2)  0.08658    0.04850   1.785    0.075 .  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 12.91 on 385 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3795,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3762 
F-statistic: 117.7 on 2 and 385 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()











5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)


   ring   n
1  Core  80
2 Inner 136
3 Outer 172


Code
m_cat <- lm(y ~ ring, data = tracts)
summary(m_cat)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ ring, data = tracts)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-33.837 -10.429  -1.548   8.576  42.791 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   38.635      1.523  25.368   <2e-16 ***
ringInner     -3.710      1.919  -1.933   0.0539 .  
ringOuter    -20.431      1.843 -11.083   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 13.62 on 385 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3097,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3061 
F-statistic: 86.35 on 2 and 385 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").

Try at least one of each: a log, a squared term, and a categorical variable. Choose which variables to transform based on your plots, not at random. Log each model.

  renter_pct + dist_bus_stop_mi

    model = "m5",
    added = "Log of median income",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_log, tracts),
    notes = "Tests whether a log transformation of income improves prediction"

  dist_bus_stop_mi + I(dist_bus_stop_mi^2)

  add_row(
    model = "m6",
    added = "Squared bus-stop distance",
    cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_sq, tracts),
    notes = "Tests for a curved relationship between transit distance and vehicle ownership"

title: Verify the Claim: White Philidelphians Living in Higher Rates of Poverty?
text:
Alfred Lubrano reported on changes in poverty and inequality across Philadelphia neighborhoods in 2018, using American Community Survey (ACS) estimates. The article shows large differences in poverty between neighborhoods. This analysis tests whether observed changes between the two periods are statistically distinguishable from zero. I then use the results and the uncertainty associated with the estimates to evaluate how strongly the article’s claims can be supported.
Source


The article cites the U.S. Census Bureau’s 5-Year American Community Survey as its source and compares the 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 periods. The article does not say the exact ACS variables it used, but I assume that its poverty comparisons are based on the number of people below the poverty level relative to the total sample. I therefore use ACS table B17001, with B17001_001 being the total sample and B17001_002 being the population below the poverty level. I calculate the poverty rate for each Philadelphia census tract as the estimated population below poverty divided by the total population. I also calculate the margin of error for each poverty-rate estimate, rather than using the margin of error for the poverty count alone. I then calculate the coefficient of variation (CV) to evaluate reliability, following these thresholds: CV values below 12% are considered reliable, values from 12% to 40% are somewhat reliable, and values above 40% are unreliable. The two ACS periods do not overlap in their five-year time windows: 2006-2010 and 2013-2017. Because of this, the differences between the estimates can be interpreted as changes between two distinct periods. They should still be interpreted with the uncertainty associated with each estimate.

The next step is to see if the difference between the two poverty-rate estimates represents a statistically significant change or could instead be explained by sampling uncertainty. For each census tract, I calculate the change in poverty rate between 2006-2010 and 2013-2017 and calculate a margin of error for that change by combining the uncertainty from both estimates. I use the 90% confidence interval, consistent with the ACS margin of error, to determine whether each change is statistically distinguishable from zero.

  select(
    GEOID,
    NAME,
    poverty_rate_2010 = poverty_rate,
    poverty_moe_2010 = poverty_moe

    poverty_rate_2017 %>%
      select(
        GEOID,
        poverty_rate_2017 = poverty_rate,
        poverty_moe_2017 = poverty_moe
      ),
    by = "GEOID"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    change = poverty_rate_2017 - poverty_rate_2010
  )




Code

  mutate(
    se_2010 = poverty_moe_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2017 = poverty_moe_2017 / 1.645,
    se_change = sqrt(se_2010^2 + se_2017^2),
    change_moe = se_change * 1.645
  )




Code

  mutate(
    lower = change - change_moe,
    upper = change + change_moe
  )




Code
poverty_change <- poverty_change %>%
  mutate(
    significant = case_when(
      lower > 0 ~ "Increase",
      upper < 0 ~ "Decrease",
      TRUE ~ "No detectable change"
    )
  )










Figure 1: The 20 largest statistically detectable changes in census-tract poverty rates between 2006-2010 and 2013-2017, with error bars showing the 90% margin of error.





The results suggest that changes in poverty rates were not widespread across Philadelphia census tracts. Some tracts show changes large enough to be statistically distinguishable from zero, but the majority of tracts do not have a detectable change once the margins of error are taken into account. This distinction is important because subtracting one ACS estimate from another can make a change appear meaningful even when the uncertainty surrounding the estimates is large enough that the true change could be zero. The reliability analysis provides context for interpreting the results. ACS estimates are based on samples rather than a complete count of the population, so the precision of the poverty-rate estimates varies across census tracts. Smaller populations are less precise estimates, which can produce larger coefficients of variation. The observed changes provide evidence of some tract-level change, but they do not support the conclusion that poverty changed substantially throughout Philadelphia. The results suggest that the claims about neighborhood change really need to account for the uncertainty surrounding the ACS estimates.



The ACS data support the article’s broader claim that poverty is unevenly distributed across Philadelphia. The tract-level estimates show substantial differences in poverty rates between census tracts during 2013-2017. Some tracts have very high poverty rates while others have much lower rates. This pattern is consistent with the article’s description of a large economic divide between Philadelphia neighborhoods. The distribution of poverty across tracts supports the article’s broader argument that economic inequality is geographically determined within the city. The data do not provide enough evidence to conclude that poverty broadly increased or decreased across Philadelphia between 2006-2010 and 2013-2017. After accounting for the margin of error of both ACS estimates, of the 376 census tracts with defined poverty rates in both periods, most show no statistically detectable change; An observed difference in a tract’s poverty rate is not necessarily evidence of a real change, it may be explained by sampling uncertainty. The data do not support a broad conclusion that poverty substantially changed throughout Philadelphia during this period.








Figure 2: Number of Philadelphia census tracts showing a statistically detectable increase, decrease, or no detectable change in poverty rates between 2006-2010 and 2013-2017.





The article uses Philadelphia neighborhood names such as Fairhill and Schuylkill-Southwest Center City, but it doesn’t say which census tracts were included in each neighborhood or provide the exact method used to aggregate the ACS data into those neighborhood boundaries (considering they aren’t officially defined). I can reproduce the underlying ACS estimates at the census-tract level, but I cannot determine exactly which tracts were combined to produce the article’s neighborhood-level estimates. The specific numerical changes attributed to individual neighborhoods cannot be directly verified from the information provided by the article.



New five-year estimates from the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey show that Philadelphia continues to experience substantial geographic inequality in poverty. The 2013-2017 estimates reveal large differences in poverty rates across census tracts, consistent with the city’s persistent economic divide. In comparison with the 2006-2010 estimates provide less evidence that poverty broadly changed across the city. After accounting for the margins of error, most census tracts show no statistically detectable change in their poverty rates. The results suggest that Philadelphia remained highly unequal, but they do not support the conclusion that poverty increased or decreased substantially throughout the city. Changes in individual tracts should be interpreted cautiously because ACS estimates are based on samples. (Adjusted from the article)

    change_moe = se_change * 1.645
  )




Code
poverty_change <- poverty_change %>%
  mutate(
    lower = change - change_moe,
    upper = change + change_moe
  )




Code
poverty_change <- poverty_change %>%
  mutate(
    significant = case_when(
      lower > 0 ~ "Increase",
      upper < 0 ~ "Decrease",
      TRUE ~ "No detectable change"
    )
  )










Figure 1: The 20 largest statistically detectable changes in census-tract poverty rates between 2006-2010 and 2013-2017, with error bars showing the 90% margin of error.





The results suggest that changes in poverty rates were not widespread across Philadelphia census tracts. Some tracts show changes large enough to be statistically distinguishable from zero, but the majority of tracts do not have a detectable change once the margins of error are taken into account. This distinction is important because subtracting one ACS estimate from another can make a change appear meaningful even when the uncertainty surrounding the estimates is large enough that the true change could be zero. The reliability analysis provides context for interpreting the results. ACS estimates are based on samples rather than a complete count of the population, so the precision of the poverty-rate estimates varies across census tracts. Smaller populations are less precise estimates, which can produce larger coefficients of variation. The observed changes provide evidence of some tract-level change, but they do not support the conclusion that poverty changed substantially throughout Philadelphia. The results suggest that the claims about neighborhood change really need to account for the uncertainty surrounding the ACS estimates.

title: Verify the Claim: White Philidelphians Living in Higher Rates of Poverty?
text:
The ACS data support the article’s broader claim that poverty is unevenly distributed across Philadelphia. The tract-level estimates show substantial differences in poverty rates between census tracts during 2013-2017. Some tracts have very high poverty rates while others have much lower rates. This pattern is consistent with the article’s description of a large economic divide between Philadelphia neighborhoods. The distribution of poverty across tracts supports the article’s broader argument that economic inequality is geographically determined within the city. The data do not provide enough evidence to conclude that poverty broadly increased or decreased across Philadelphia between 2006-2010 and 2013-2017. After accounting for the margin of error of both ACS estimates, of the 376 census tracts with defined poverty rates in both periods, most show no statistically detectable change; An observed difference in a tract’s poverty rate is not necessarily evidence of a real change, it may be explained by sampling uncertainty. The data do not support a broad conclusion that poverty substantially changed throughout Philadelphia during this period.








Figure 2: Number of Philadelphia census tracts showing a statistically detectable increase, decrease, or no detectable change in poverty rates between 2006-2010 and 2013-2017.





The article uses Philadelphia neighborhood names such as Fairhill and Schuylkill-Southwest Center City, but it doesn’t say which census tracts were included in each neighborhood or provide the exact method used to aggregate the ACS data into those neighborhood boundaries (considering they aren’t officially defined). I can reproduce the underlying ACS estimates at the census-tract level, but I cannot determine exactly which tracts were combined to produce the article’s neighborhood-level estimates. The specific numerical changes attributed to individual neighborhoods cannot be directly verified from the information provided by the article.

The 2013-2017 estimates reveal large differences in poverty rates across census tracts, consistent with the city’s persistent economic divide. In comparison with the 2006-2010 estimates provide less evidence that poverty broadly changed across the city. After accounting for the margins of error, most census tracts show no statistically detectable change in their poverty rates. title: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I examine median gross rent across counties in Oregon. I want to understand which communities have the most and least reliable rent estimates and whether some counties have greater uncertainty in their Census data than others.

Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "OR"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25064_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

title: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%

The one low confidence county has a much smaller population of about 2,002 people. The results show that smaller counties tend to have less reliable estimates and larger margins of error.

title: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The communities we know the least about in this analysis are the smaller counties in Oregon, which have the largest margins of error relative to their median gross rent estimates. Gilliam County has the highest margin of error at 15.31%, followed by Sherman County at 14.07% and Wheeler County at 13.43%. Morrow County and Hood River County also have relatively high margins of error, at 11.98% and 10.72%, respectively. These results suggest that the reliability of ACS estimates is related to the size of the communities being measured. The ACS does not collect information from every household. It uses a sample to estimate characteristics for larger populations. There are fewer households in smaller counties to be included in the sample, meaning that individual responses have a greater effect on the overall estimate. This causes larger margins of error for the reported median gross rent. The high-confidence counties in my analysis have an average population of about 197,743, compared with only 18,790 for moderate-confidence counties and 2,002 for the one low-confidence county. This uncertainty could create problems if a state agency used these estimates to allocate housing-related funding while treating every county’s number as equally reliable. Smaller counties could receive too much or too little funding based on an estimate that is relatively uncertain. This could particularly hurt rural communities, such as in Gillian County, where limited resources and smaller populations already make it harder to accurately identify housing needs.

text:
Part 7: Reflection
Distance to the nearest stop lowered CV RMSE the most of the individual spatial features, from 12.44 for the baseline to 10.98, probably because it measures how close residents are to transit, which plausibly shapes whether a household needs a car. The raw stop count disappointed me most (12.35), since a count mostly tracks tract size rather than access, and the squared distance term added little (10.90), suggesting the relationship is close to linear. The City Hall distance categories (10.32) and logged income (10.76) each helped moderately, and combining them produced the final model’s 10.03. For distance, β̂ = −0.98: holding income, age, renter share, and City Hall ring constant, tracts one mile farther from the nearest stop have a 0.98 percentage-point lower share of households without a vehicle. For ŷ, a tract with otherwise typical characteristics and a stop 0.1 miles away is predicted to have 30.7% of households with no vehicle, versus 30.3% at 0.5 miles, a small gap because most tracts are close to a stop. On the final residual map, red clusters remain in North Philadelphia, parts of West Philadelphia, and Center City/South Philadelphia, where actual vehicle-free rates exceed predictions, so I would next measure transit service frequency and off-street parking availability in dense row house neighborhoods. Finally, very little of the remaining error looks like survey noise: the largest misses, 20 to 30 points, occur at low outcome CVs of about 0.1% to 0.3%, where ACS estimates are most precise, and the smoothed line does not rise as CV increases, so the leftover error mostly reflects what the model leaves out rather than uncertainty in the ACS estimate.
